extracted.intended_audience: covered entities (health programs and activities), health care providers, health system administrators, and their legal/compliance advisors subject to Section 1557 (OCR/HHS)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards implementing Section 1557's prohibition on discrimination on the basis of sex for health programs and activities, focused on equal program access, gender-affirming care, sex-separated programs/facilities, and related exceptions. Useful for covered entities, providers, and counsel assessing policies and practices for compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: General obligation to provide equal access without sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities must provide individuals equal access to the covered entity's health programs or activities without discrimination on the basis of sex (proposed § 92.206(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a broad, general prohibition; the rule's other paragraphs provide examples of prohibited conduct but do not limit the general obligation. Determinations are often context-specific and fact-intensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on denying or limiting health services based on sex characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A covered entity may not deny or limit health services, including services offered exclusively to individuals of one sex, to an individual based on the individual's sex assigned at birth, gender identity, or gender otherwise recorded (§ 92.206(b)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes services offered exclusively to one sex; case-by-case evaluation will determine whether a denial or limitation constitutes prohibited discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on restricting clinicians based on patient's sex characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities may not deny or limit a health care professional's ability to provide health services on the basis of a patient's sex assigned at birth, gender identity, or gender otherwise recorded (§ 92.206(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prohibits restrictions on individual providers (e.g., limitations that prevent prescribing or providing care) where the restriction is based on the patient's sex characteristics and has the effect of discriminating against patients. Employment practices are generally outside this rule, but employees are protected against retaliation under §§ 92.303–92.304.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on sex-based separation/treatment that causes more-than-de-minimis harm
rubrics_metrics.description: A covered entity may not apply any policy or practice of treating individuals differently or separating them on the basis of sex in a manner that subjects any individual to more than de minimis harm (§ 92.206(b)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule distinguishes permissible sex-based distinctions (those causing only de minimis impact) from prohibited ones (more-than-de-minimis harm). Examples include sex-separated programs and facilities: they are allowed so long as they do not subject anyone to more-than-de-minimis harm. OCR will evaluate harm fact-specifically. Courts have held safety and privacy can be protected without excluding transgender individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on denying or limiting gender-affirming care when denial is based on sex characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A covered entity may not deny or limit health services sought for the purpose of gender-affirming care that the covered entity would provide to a person for other purposes if the denial or limitation is based on a patient's sex assigned at birth, gender identity, or gender otherwise recorded (§ 92.206(b)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine whether a covered entity violated § 1557 by denying gender-affirming care, OCR may consider evidence such as provider statements, prior provision of similar care, and documentation of scope of practice. The rule does not require entities to provide gender-affirming care categorically; it prohibits denial when motivated by a prohibited basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate nondiscriminatory clinical appropriateness exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in § 92.206 requires the provision of any health service where the covered entity has a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for denying or limiting that service, including where the covered entity reasonably determines that such health service is not clinically appropriate for that particular individual (§ 92.206(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 1557 does not compel a specific standard of care or interfere with individualized clinical judgment. Entities may articulate legitimate nondiscriminatory bases for challenged practices, but such bases cannot be pretextual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated examples do not limit general prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: The enumeration of specific forms of discrimination in paragraph (b) does not limit the general applicability of the prohibition in paragraph (a) (§ 92.206(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The listed prohibitions are illustrative; other forms of sex discrimination may violate § 92.101(a)(1) even if not specifically enumerated in § 92.206(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: De minimis-harm threshold for permissible sex-based distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex-based distinctions are permissible where they do not cause more than de minimis harm; treating individuals differently on the basis of sex constitutes discrimination where it imposes more-than-de-minimis harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR finalizes this standard as the appropriate threshold. The rule does not prohibit all sex-based distinctions or differential treatment; the assessment of harm is fact-specific. This standard is consistent with case law cited (including Bostock) and allows for sex-specific clinical trials when sex is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of sex-specific research/clinical trials when scientifically justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Health research and clinical trial protocols are not prohibited from specifying an individual's sex consistent with their reproductive, anatomical, and genetic characteristics where those characteristics are relevant to the clinical trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should be able to demonstrate necessary justifications for nondiscriminatory research distinctions. OCR recognizes that sex is an important biological variable in medicine and that sex-specific trials can be appropriate when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of medically relevant inquiries and harassment threshold for questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Providers may ask medically relevant questions about a patient's anatomy or medical history in the course of providing care; such inquiries are not per se discriminatory. However, if questions are irrelevant to assessing the condition or are repeated after the patient objects, they may constitute harassment based on sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: asking about possible pregnancy in a patient presenting with ectopic pregnancy symptoms is appropriate. Harassment claims will be evaluated case-by-case for whether conduct was 'sufficiently severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive.' Isolated, non-animus incidents are unlikely to meet the harassment standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standards for determining whether gender-affirming care is ordinarily provided
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR may consider statements by the provider, information showing the provider has provided similar care in the past, or documentation regarding the provider's scope of practice as evidence that the type of care is ordinarily provided by the covered entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence can establish that a denial of gender-affirming care was based on a prohibited characteristic rather than legitimate clinical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrimination caused by restrictions on providers (secondary effects) prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibited discrimination may take the form of restrictions on individual providers (e.g., restricting an attending physician from providing services) where such restrictions are imposed based on a patient's gender identity or sex assigned at birth and have the effect of discriminating against patients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision is modeled on title VI language and clarifies that restrictions on providers are prohibited only insofar as they result in discrimination against individuals in a covered health program or activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of sexual orientation and gender identity under sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1557 and this rule prohibit discrimination on the basis of sex, including sex characteristics, sexual orientation, and gender identity; barriers to fertility or other services that categorically deny care to same-sex couples or individuals on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity may violate § 1557.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR anticipates categorical denials of routinely provided services to same-sex couples on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity may constitute discrimination; OCR declines to add additional specific regulatory text enumerating fertility protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit inclusion of sex characteristics (including intersex traits) under sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule makes explicit in regulatory text that sex discrimination includes discrimination based on sex characteristics, including intersex traits, as reflected in § 92.101(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR appreciates commenters noting the impacts on intersex people and clarifies the coverage in regulatory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious freedom and conscience protections/exemptions preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule recognizes Federal conscience protections; nothing in the Act shall be construed to affect Federal laws regarding conscience protection, willingness or refusal to provide abortion, or related discrimination (42 U.S.C. 18023(c)(2)(A)). Recipients may rely on religious freedom or conscience protections directly (§ 92.3(c)) or seek an assurance/exemption (§ 92.302(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will respect guarantees of Federal religious freedom and conscience laws; certain applications of the rule are not required insofar as they would violate those laws. Further discussion in §§ 92.208 and 92.302.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule does not set clinical standards of care or compel specific treatments
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1557 prohibits discrimination and does not (and cannot) require a specific standard of care or course of treatment for any individual, nor interfere with individualized clinical judgment about appropriate care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR defers to clinicians' judgment about medical appropriateness and expertise. The rule allows entities to justify nondiscriminatory clinical decisions, but cannot be used to mask discrimination behind clinical policies or criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee protections against retaliation separate from employment practice regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the rule does not apply to employment practices generally (§ 92.2(b)), employees of covered entities remain protected against retaliation as provided in §§ 92.303 and 92.304; OCR must determine jurisdiction before investigating State licensure boards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction means employer personnel policies may fall outside the rule, but retaliation protections still apply to employees when linked to discrimination in a covered health program or activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: No regulatory definition of gender-affirming care; examples provided
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR declines to provide a regulatory definition for 'gender-affirming care'; when used in §§ 92.206 and 92.207 it generally refers to care designed to treat gender dysphoria that may include counseling, hormone therapy, surgery, and other related services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule does not categorically require provision of gender-affirming care. OCR considered comments both supporting and opposing gender-affirming care but did not change regulatory text to define or expand obligations.
